stories.title: Angela Gentry of JLL: 5 Questions
stories.excerpt: Angela Gentry has carved out her own spot in New York City’s commercial real estate scene. In 2022, Gentry, who at the time had more than 20 years of experience in the field, joined JLL in a role specifically created for her: executive managing director of sales and platform for the New York tri-state area. She describes the role as being the “ultimate Switzerland” for the brokerage, in that she focused on what was best for both the firm and its clients when it came to leasing and sales. Then in May, Gentry was promoted to vice chairman of leasing advisory for the New York tri-state region, a position that doesn’t yet exist in a similar way in JLL’s other markets. Gentry’s job is to take what JLL does really well in New York City and scale it nationally. And what the firm’s been doing well in New York City is deals, deals, deals. In terms of sales, the firm just facilitated the $58 million sale of a development site in Downtown Brooklyn and the $31 million sale of a shopping center in Midwood, Brooklyn. As for leases, the firm’s certainly riding the artificial intelligence wave, as it’s had a hand in several recent tech deals, including a 98,420-square-foot deal for AI firm Legora at SL Green Realty’s 11 Madison Avenue and a 13,754-square-foot lease for Genius AI at ZG Capital Partners’ 838 Broadway. Commercial Observer sat down with Gentry on Monday to discuss her work at JLL and what she’s seeing in the city’s office market as AI tenants take more and more space. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: You joined JLL in 2022 and took a position created specifically for you. What was unique about that role? Angela Gentry: When I was first hired at JLL, I was the senior director for sales enablement. I was brought in to stand it up for the New York tri-state area. stories.summary: JLL's leadership and transactional momentum in New York markets underscore brokerage strength in deal-making and leasing advisory. Recent sales include a $58M development site in Downtown Brooklyn and $31M retail in Midwood, with AI-sector leasing activity accelerating. The firm is leveraging its New York playbook nationally through new leadership roles focused on scaling advisory services.

stories.title: New York State Gets One More Shot at Opportunity Zones
stories.excerpt: When equity for ground-up development disappeared in 2022, Opportunity Zone capital didn’t. Four years later that dynamic is largely the same. But Congress has now rewritten the Opportunity Zone (OZ) program, and New York has just over 60 days to decide where the next decade of OZ capital can go. The reason Opportunity Zone funds kept investing anyway is because the statute obligated them to deploy into qualifying tracts or forfeit the benefit. In addition, OZ capital (a) has a mandatory 10-year investment horizon, which suits development projects in emerging neighborhoods much better than opportunistic capital, which typically has a three- to five-year time horizon; and (b) it is priced less expensively by allocators because of its tax-advantaged treatment. Jeffrey Deitrich. In 2022, as conventional equity pulled back from ground-up development, my platform closed equity investments into more than 2,000 units of multifamily construction across the country. We have since funded close to 5,000 housing units. With inflation and interest rates repricing the capital stack, OZ equity was the money that showed up. That is the lesson worth carrying into the next round. OZ 1.0 proved that private equity under a statutory obligation keeps investing when conventional capital retreats. OZ 2.0 gives cities a short window to better aim that capital where it’s needed. Leaders who treat the next 60 days as a formality will spend the following decade watching the money go elsewhere. New York designated 514 census tracts in 2018 as qualifying Opportunity Zones. The Treasury’s latest accounting puts national OZ investment at $112 billion through 2024, up from $44 billion through 2020. New York accounted for roughly $8.2 billion of it, behind only California and Florida. On volume, the state did well. Targeting is the harder verdict. Critics predicted from the start that the money would land in neighborhoods that didn’t need it. In New York City, they were partly right. OZ
bullets: Congress rewrites Opportunity Zone program; New York has 60 days to nominate tracts.
OZ capital funded 5,000+ multifamily units nationwide since 2022 despite equity market freeze.
OZ's 10-year horizon and tax-advantaged pricing ideal for ground-up development in emerging neighborhoods.
stories.summary: The Opportunity Zone program has been restructured by Congress, forcing New York to quickly redefine eligible investment tracts over the next 60 days. OZ capital has deployed nearly $5,000 multifamily units since 2022, proving resilient when conventional development equity disappeared. The program's 10-year investment mandate and tax benefits make it uniquely suited to long-cycle ground-up development in emerging neighborhoods.
stories.impact: OZ capital reallocation directly affects New York State multifamily development feasibility and site eligibility. Developers should monitor which NY tracts are designated in the next 60 days; OZ-designated sites will attract cheaper, longer-duration equity capital, improving underwriting returns on ground-up projects in secondary/emerging submarkets across the state.

stories.title: Prosper and Versluys Close $50M Land Deal for $650M Miami Condo Tower
stories.excerpt: Prosper Group and Versluys Group have paid $50 million for a development site in Miami’s Brickell district, where they plan to build a $650 million condo tower, the joint venture announced. The 1-acre assemblage includes three parcels: one along the Miami River, with more than 300 feet of water frontage, as well as two adjacent inland spots at 66 Southwest Sixth Street and 625 Southwest First Avenue, near the Brickell City Center mixed-use complex. The joint venture plans to develop a 60-story waterfront high-rise with 181 condos. Vaster provided a $30.5 million loan for the acquisition, which has been under contract for at least eight months. The sellers, developers Two Roads Development and Newgard Development Group, are currently building another luxury complex on a neighboring lot at 99 Southwest Seventh Street. Last year, the joint venture nabbed a $513 million financing package for the construction of two condo towers: a 46-story, 422-unit building branded after the Standard Hotel and the 44-stories, 362-unit Lofty Brickell building. The Brickell project marks the first U.S. endeavor for Belgian developer Versluys Group, which was founded in 1908. Prosper, led and founded by former Wall Street financier Jay Roberts, has made inroads in Miami real estate in recent years, though no projects have reached the construction phase yet. Brickell is seeing a rush of luxury development. Along the bayfront, billionaire hedge funder Ken Griffin is planning to build a mixed-use complex, including a 54-story office skyscraper. The Cipriani-branded and St Regis-branded condo projects remain under construction. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Prosper Group and Versluys Group acquire 1-acre Miami Brickell site for $50M; plan $650M condo tower.
Joint venture secures $30.5M acquisition loan from Vaster; 60-story, 181-unit waterfront high-rise planned.
Site includes 300+ feet Miami River frontage; sellers Two Roads and Newgard building adjacent luxury complex.
stories.summary: Prosper Group and Versluys Group closed a $50M land acquisition in Miami's Brickell district for a proposed $650M condo tower with 181 units. The 1-acre waterfront assemblage (three parcels) includes 300+ feet of Miami River frontage adjacent to Brickell City Center. Vaster provided $30.5M acquisition financing; the deal follows the JV's earlier $513M construction financing for two condo towers (46-story, 422-unit and an unnamed second tower).
stories.impact: Condo development, not rental multifamily. Limited direct impact on apartment supply/demand. However, the aggressive waterfront acquisition and construction financing signal strong capital availability and demand for luxury residential in Miami Brickell; competitive land pricing may inflate land costs for nearby rental projects.

stories.title: Hawkins Way, Varde Acquire East Village Student Housing
stories.excerpt: Hawkins Way Capital and joint venture partner Varde Partners completed the acquisition of 81 E. 3rd St., a student housing property located in Manhattan’s East Village. Acquired for $28 million, the off-market transaction marks a strategic addition to the growing FOUND Study student housing portfolio and expands the platform’s presence in one of New York City’s most sought-after neighborhoods. The property features apartment-style layouts that offer an enhanced living experience, compared to traditional dormitory accommodations, according to Hawkins Way. Its flexible design also provides long-term optionality, with the ability to serve both student housing and conventional multifamily uses. “The East Village has long been a market we have targeted, given its concentration of students, proximity to leading universities, and enduring real estate fundamentals,” said Ross Walker, managing partner, Hawkins Way. “This acquisition expands our JV’s presence in one of Manhattan’s most dynamic neighborhoods and reinforces our strategy of investing in well-located urban student housing assets positioned to benefit from sustained demand.” Join the industry’s top multifamily decision-makers at Connect Apartments on September 22 in LA. stories.summary: Hawkins Way Capital and Varde Partners completed a $28M off-market acquisition of a 81 E. 3rd St. student housing property in Manhattan's East Village for the FOUND Study platform. The property features apartment-style units with optionality for both student housing and conventional multifamily conversion. The acquisition expands the platform's presence in a neighborhood with sustained demand from university proximity and strong real estate fundamentals.
stories.impact: Student housing acquisition, not conventional rental multifamily development. Signals investor confidence in NYC's East Village submarket and underscores dual-use asset flexibility. Indirect signal: if student housing operators are aggressively acquiring (off-market, $28M), rental fundamentals in East Village remain resilient and may support higher rents for standard multifamily nearby.

stories.title: Former Blue Shield of CA Offices Trade for Residential Conversion
stories.excerpt: NAI Capital Commercial executive managing director Ryan Campbell, SIOR, represented The Olson Company in its $24,850,000 acquisition of a 7.9-acre office campus at 601 Potrero Grande Dr. and 2100 Saturn St. in Monterey Park. The campus includes two office buildings totaling 120,191 square feet. The buyer plans to redevelop the property into a new residential community. Originally built in 1980, the campus was previously owned and occupied by Blue Shield of California. Andrew Harper, Jeff Bramson, and Will Poulsen of JLL represented the seller. “This acquisition reflects the continued shift toward repositioning well-located office properties into much-needed housing throughout the San Gabriel Valley,” said Campbell. “Large infill redevelopment opportunities like this are increasingly rare. The size, location, and long-term potential of this campus make it exceptionally well-suited to deliver new housing while transforming an underutilized office property into a vibrant residential community.” Stay ahead of the multifamily market at Connect Apartments. bullets: Olson Company acquires former Blue Shield of CA office campus (120,191 SF) in Monterey Park for $24.85M.
7.9-acre infill site (601 Potrero Grande Dr. and 2100 Saturn St.) planned for residential redevelopment.

stories.summary: The Olson Company acquired a 7.9-acre office campus (two buildings, 120,191 SF) formerly occupied by Blue Shield of California in Monterey Park for $24.85M, planning residential conversion. The property was originally constructed in 1980 and sits as an underutilized office asset. The acquisition exemplifies the broader trend of repositioning suburban office campuses into housing across greater Los Angeles.
stories.impact: Office-to-residential conversion in Monterey Park/San Gabriel Valley signals accelerating demand for housing in infill locations and limited new ground-up sites. For Trammell Crow, this indicates: (1) large, entitled conversion opportunities exist in SGV/mid-LA submarkets; (2) office-to-residential conversion may prove cheaper/faster than ground-up on constrained infill sites; (3) land scarcity is driving builders to repositioning strategies, potentially reducing new-construction supply competition in the valley.

stories.title: JAMS Relocating New York Offices to 3 Times Square
stories.excerpt: Rudin has secured an agreement with JAMS, a provider of alternative dispute resolution services, to relocate its New York Resolution Center to 3 Times Square. The tenant will occupy 55,335 square feet across the entirety of the building’s top two floors. As part of the 11-year lease, JAMS is expected to move from its current offices at 620 Eighth Ave. in the fourth quarter of 2027. “JAMS’ major commitment to 3 Times Square underscores the market’s continued appetite for top-quality, well-located properties with premier amenity programs,” said Michael Rudin, co-CEO of Rudin. “JAMS joins a diverse roster of high-caliber companies who value vibrant, transit-connected Midtown Manhattan office destinations.” Rudin was represented in-house by Kevin Daly along with the Cushman & Wakefield team of Ron LoRusso, Lou D’Avanzo, John Cefaly, Michael Burgio, Dan Organ and Paige Engeldrum. Ken Rapp, Brendan Herlihy and Ron Wade of CBRE represented JAMS. The post JAMS Relocating New York Offices to 3 Times Square appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: JAMS relocates New York Resolution Center to 3 Times Square; signs 11-year lease for 55,335 SF.
Tenant occupies top two floors; move from 620 Eighth Ave. scheduled for Q4 2027.
Rudin-owned asset continues to attract high-quality tenants; lease reflects strong Manhattan office demand.
stories.summary: Rudin secured an 11-year office lease with JAMS (alternative dispute resolution provider) for 55,335 SF across the top two floors of 3 Times Square. JAMS will relocate from its current offices at 620 Eighth Ave. in Q4 2027. The deal underscores continued tenant demand for premier, transit-connected Manhattan office space with strong amenities.
stories.impact: Office leasing in Midtown Manhattan does not directly affect multifamily supply, demand, or capital. Marginal signal: strong office leasing in Times Square may support continued employment and foot traffic in Midtown, sustaining rental demand in nearby residential corridors (Hudson Yards, Midtown residential submarkets), but this is an indirect and minor effect.

stories.title: Shopoff Sells Site of Proposed Newport Beach Condo Development
stories.excerpt: Shopoff Realty Investments has sold a proposed 1.06-acre condominium development, Park Palm in Newport Beach, to Shea Homes for an undisclosed sum. The property is part of Shopoff’s master plan community, Uptown Newport Village, and is entitled for 23 townhomes. Shopoff acquired the 25-acre Uptown Newport Village site in December 2010. The firm set out to repurpose the land for a mixed-use residential village, rather than maintain its prior office and industrial uses. In 2013, Shopoff completed the entitlement process, allowing for master development to include 1,244 residential units, 11,500 square feet of commercial/retail space and two one-acre parks. Phase I of the project has seen multiple developments completed, beginning with One Uptown Newport in 2019. Park Palm, which has been entitled for 23 townhomes, will round out Phase I. Construction on Park Palm is anticipated to begin in 2027, with completion expected in 2028-2029. The site is entitled for 23 townhomes, with construction slated for 2027 and completion in 2028-2029. The broader Uptown Newport Village master plan allows for 1,244 residential units across the 25-acre site, with Phase I substantially completed.
stories.impact: For-sale townhome development, not rental multifamily. Limited direct impact. However, the sale to Shea Homes and 2027-2028 construction timeline signal continued builder appetite for entitled Orange County sites; rental developers should note that for-sale and rental markets are competing for prime Newport Beach infill locations, potentially inflating land costs.

stories.title: JLL Lists Staten Island Waterfront Development for $45M
stories.excerpt: JLL Capital Markets has been retained by Traingle Equities as sales advisor for Lighthouse Point, a newly completed, transit-oriented, Class A multifamily waterfront development located at 5 Bay St. in the St. George neighborhood of Staten Island. The asking price is $45 million. Lighthouse Point is a mixed-use development situated adjacent to the Staten Island Ferry Terminal. Occupying the site of the historic U.S. Lighthouse Service’s General Depot, the recently completed first phase features 115 residential units. The JLL Capital Markets Investment Sales and Advisory team representing the seller is led by senior managing directors Rob Hinckley and Jeff Julien, managing director Steven Rutman and director Devon Warren. “Lighthouse Point presents a rare opportunity in today’s market,” said Warren. “It’s a well-conceived project in a market where new development opportunities are increasingly limited, and we think buyers will recognize both the quality of what’s been built and the potential that’s still ahead.” Where the apartment industry connects. The mixed-use project, located at 5 Bay St. adjacent to the Staten Island Ferry Terminal, features 115 residential units in its first phase. The asset occupies the historic site of the U.S. Lighthouse Service General Depot and represents a rare new-development opportunity in a constrained market.
stories.impact: Asset sale (not development pipeline impact). However, $45M ask price for 115-unit Phase 1 implies ~$391K per unit in valuation, signaling strong cap rates and buyer appetite for transit-oriented Staten Island multifamily. Indicates waterfront/transit-oriented assets in emerging outer-borough NYC markets command premium pricing and competition, which may elevate land/development costs for competing projects in St. George and similar submarkets.

stories.title: Brookfield Asset Management Raises Record $77B in Q2
stories.excerpt: Brookfield Asset Management raised a company record $77 billion in the second quarter of 2026, bringing its assets under management to more than $1 trillion, the investment firm reported in an earnings call Wednesday. Year-to-date, the investor has brought in $98 billion, more than half of what Brookfield raised for all last year. It also deployed $21 billion this past quarter. Brookfield’s seventh flagship private equity fund raised $6.7 billion during the quarter, while its sixth flagship infrastructure fund brought in $9.3 billion, putting both on pace to become the largest funds of their respective vintages. The firm also secured $5 billion in commitments for its first AI Infrastructure Fund. In another AI-focused venture, Brookfield increased its financing framework with Bloom Energy for AI infrastructure power projects to $25 billion, up from the $5 billion commitment announced in October 2025. “We can source and entitle power land, develop and operate large-scale AI factories, deliver behind-the-meter and baseload power, provide contracted compute, and pursue partnerships with some of the major stakeholders, including semiconductor players and hyperscalers,” said Sikander Rashid, Brookfield’s global head of AI infrastructure. “Not many firms can bring all of that together.” On the real estate front, Brookfield also raised $4.3 billion across segment funds and deployed $5.2 billion, buying a privately held U.S. manufactured-home portfolio and the taking private of an outdoor industrial storage portfolio. Brookfield also completed its purchase of Oaktree, buying the remaining 26 percent stake for about $3 billion. bullets: Brookfield Asset Management raises record $77B in Q2 2026; YTD total $98B; AUM exceeds $1 trillion.

stories.summary: Brookfield Asset Management raised a company-record $77B in Q2 2026, bringing year-to-date fundraising to $98B and total AUM to over $1 trillion. The firm's flagship private equity and infrastructure funds are tracking to become the largest of their respective vintages. Brookfield also secured $5B in commitments for its inaugural AI Infrastructure Fund and expanded its Bloom Energy financing framework to $25B for AI power infrastructure.
stories.impact: Brookfield's record capital raise signals strong institutional appetite for large-scale infrastructure and alternative assets, which may compete with multifamily for institutional capital and development opportunities. However, Brookfield's AI infrastructure focus (power, data centers) suggests capital is flowing away from traditional residential development toward energy/tech infrastructure, potentially freeing up multifamily-focused equity and reducing capital competition for apartment projects.

stories.title: Return-to-Office Gained New Momentum in First Half of 2026: Report
stories.excerpt: U.S. office attendance is on the rise, but the return-to-office trend remains a tale of two cities. In the first half of 2026, office visits nationwide rose 6 percent year-over-year, and achieved the narrowest first-half gap from pre-pandemic levels thus far, data from foot-traffic tracker Placer.ai shows. The six-month period of foot traffic marked acceleration from the 1.9 percent annual uptick observed in the same period of 2025. Office attendance is far from a full and even recovery, however. U.S. office visits remain 31.2 percent below 2019 levels, according to Placer.ai’s August office market report. While Miami and New York are making strides toward baseline visitation levels, Denver and Chicago still have a long way to go. The hybrid workweek also appears here to stay –– for now. The report’s survey of 11 major U.S. markets revealed that office attendance diverges widely across geographies. Cubicles and corner offices are filling up in Miami, where attendance in the first half of the year was 11.5 percent below that of 2019. First-half attendance in Denver, on the other hand, remained more than 40 percent below 2019 levels. The “most improved” award for the period of January through June goes to West Coast hubs Los Angeles and San Francisco, with annual visitation upticks of 13 percent and 10.9 percent, respectively. The pair of cities achieved the report’s largest year-over-year gains. Hybrid workweeks have made a lasting impact on U.S. corporate culture, but the model’s popularity is waning in some markets. The country’s highest shares of Friday office attendance belong to Miami and Dallas, where roughly one in seven weekday office visits fell on a Friday. In Chicago, however, Fridays account for less than one out of every 10 office visits. This is the same city where personalized video platform Cameo announced last year a $10,000 raise for every new and existing employee that returns to its Fulton Market office four days per week. bullets: U.S. office attendance rose 6% YoY in H1 2026; narrowest first-half gap from 2019 baseline to date.

stories.summary: U.S. office attendance improved 6% year-over-year in the first half of 2026, marking the strongest first-half recovery yet, though office visits remain 31.2% below 2019 levels. Miami and New York are approaching pre-pandemic baseline visitation (Miami 11.5% below), while Denver and Chicago lag significantly (40%+ below 2019 levels). The hybrid work model persists, with substantial geographic divergence.
stories.impact: Modest net positive for multifamily in Miami and NYC. Return-to-office gains in Miami and New York support sustained office-employment demand and worker retention in those metros, supporting continued rental demand. However, persistent office underutilization (31% below 2019) and Denver/Chicago weakness signal that office-to-residential conversions will remain feasible and attractive, particularly in soft office markets—enabling Trammell Crow to pursue conversion opportunities in secondary markets where RTO momentum is weak.
